diagnosis_and_plan.preliminary_diagnosis: 1. Digital tendinitis or flexor tendonitis of the right index finger. 2. Soft tissue injury or sprain of the right index finger. 3. Possible early-stage osteoarthritis (uncommon in this age without prior injury).
diagnosis_and_plan.diagnosis_discussion: The patient is a 42-year-old female with a recent skiing injury to her right index finger, presenting with localized pain, tenderness, and limited range of motion without swelling, bruising, or deformity. The X-ray ruled out fractures or dislocations, pointing toward a soft tissue or tendon-related issue. Digital tendinitis or flexor tendonitis is a likely diagnosis given the pain with movement and localized tenderness. A soft tissue injury or sprain is also plausible, as the injury mechanism (skiing) could have caused ligamentous or soft tissue damage. Early-stage osteoarthritis is less likely but considered as a differential due to the pain with movement and localized tenderness, though this is uncommon in the absence of prior joint issues or degenerative conditions. No systemic symptoms, family history of rheumatological conditions, or prior injuries to the finger were reported, which reduces the likelihood of rheumatological or chronic degenerative conditions.
diagnosis_and_plan.treatment_plan: 1. Further evaluation: Consider an MRI or ultrasound of the right index finger to assess for soft tissue or tendon abnormalities, especially if symptoms persist or worsen. 2. Medication: Continue with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen for pain and inflammation, but consider alternative options if there is no improvement, such as acetaminophen for pain relief. If there is no response to NSAIDs, a short course of corticosteroid injections may be considered for localized inflammation. 3. Non-drug management and education: Advise the patient to avoid activities that exacerbate the pain, such as gripping or bending the finger. Recommend applying ice to the affected area for 15-20 minutes several times a day to reduce inflammation. Encourage gentle range-of-motion exercises as tolerated to prevent stiffness. Educate the patient on recognizing signs of infection (e.g., redness, warmth, swelling, fever) or worsening pain, which would require further evaluation. 4. Follow-up: Schedule a follow-up appointment in one week to reassess symptoms and consider further imaging if needed. If there is no improvement or if symptoms worsen, a referral to a hand specialist may be warranted.
